title: Sentence Types: Structure, Function and Repair

blocks.text: "After a long and exhausting journey through the flooded roads of the delta, the weary relief workers finally reached the camp." Twenty-two words — and still a simple sentence. Meanwhile "It rained, so we left" is only five words and is compound. Classification counts clauses, never words.

blocks.markdown:
Sentences are classified in two completely separate ways, and an exam question will always tell you which one it wants.

**By structure** — how many clauses, and of what kind: simple, compound, complex, compound-complex.

**By function** — what the sentence does: declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamatory.

The same sentence has one answer under each heading. "Did you finish the work before the bell rang?" is complex by structure and interrogative by function.

rows: The rain fell, but the match continued.
One main clause plus a subordinate clause
Although the fees rose, enrolment increased.
Two or more main clauses plus a subordinate clause
When the results came, the students cheered and their parents gave thanks.
blocks.caption: Classification by structure

blocks.title: *And* does not always mean compound
blocks.text: "The head girl **and** the senior prefect addressed the assembly" is simple. The *and* joins two subjects that share one verb, so there is still only one clause. A sentence is compound only when *and* joins two groups that each have their own subject and finite verb.

blocks.title: Classifying a sentence by structure
blocks.prompt: Classify by structure: "When the results were released, the students celebrated and their parents gave thanks."

steps.text: Underline every finite verb: *were released*, *celebrated*, *gave*. Three finite verbs means three clauses.
Take each clause in turn and test whether it can stand alone. *When the results were released* cannot, because of *When* — so it is subordinate.
*The students celebrated* can stand alone — main clause.
*Their parents gave thanks* can stand alone — main clause.
Tally the result: two main clauses and one subordinate clause.
Match the tally to the labels: two or more main clauses plus at least one subordinate clause is compound-complex.

blocks.answer: Compound-complex — two main clauses joined by *and*, plus one subordinate adverbial clause of time

rows: Gives a command or request; subject *you* understood
How quickly she finished the paper!
blocks.caption: Classification by function

blocks.markdown:
### Two faults examiners plant deliberately

**Sentence fragment** — a group punctuated as a sentence but lacking a main clause.
> *Wrong:* Because the generator had broken down again.
> *Right:* The hall was dark because the generator had broken down again.

**Run-on and comma splice** — two main clauses joined with nothing, or joined with only a comma.
> *Wrong:* The bus was full, we waited for the next one.
> *Right:* The bus was full, **so** we waited for the next one.
> *Also right:* The bus was full**;** we waited for the next one.

Remember that *however*, *therefore*, *nevertheless* and *moreover* are conjunctive adverbs, not conjunctions. They need a semicolon or a full stop before them, never a bare comma.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Before classifying, underline every finite verb in the sentence and remember that an auxiliary plus its main verb, such as *would subside*, counts as one. The number of underlinings is the number of clauses, and the rest of the classification follows almost automatically.

points: Structure is decided by counting clauses, never by counting words.
Simple has one clause; compound has two main clauses; complex has a main plus a subordinate clause.
Compound-complex has at least two main clauses and at least one subordinate clause.
*And* joining two subjects that share one verb leaves the sentence simple.
By function, sentences are declarative, interrogative, imperative or exclamatory.
Repair a fragment by supplying a main clause, and a comma splice by adding a conjunction or a semicolon.
